Matthew Mead
MATH-yoo MEED
proper noun
Hebrew given name Matthew, “gift of the LORD”; the surname Mead, from the Old English mæd, “a meadow.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Matthew Mead (c.1630–1699) was a Puritan minister who labored in and around London and was among those silenced by the Act of Uniformity in 1662, afterward continuing as a Nonconformist pastor at Stepney, where he gathered a large and faithful congregation. He is chiefly remembered for his searching treatise The Almost Christian Discovered, drawn from the words of Agrippa to Paul, “Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.” In it Mead anatomizes the deceptive condition of the man who goes far in the form of religion yet falls short of saving grace—who has knowledge without holiness, profession without possession, conviction without conversion. With great discernment he marks out the many ways a man may resemble a true believer and yet remain a stranger to Christ: he may hate sin and yet not forsake it, may obey much of the law and yet not be born again, may have great gifts and yet lack the one thing needful. Mead’s aim was to awaken the self-deceived from a false peace and to drive the soul to examine whether it be truly in the faith. His doctrine flows from the Reformed conviction that regeneration is the sovereign work of the Spirit and that no measure of outward religion can supply its place. The treatise remains a sharp instrument for self-examination, sparing no false hope.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A silenced Puritan minister of Stepney, author of The Almost Christian Discovered.

expand to see more

MATTHEW MEAD, English Puritan minister (c.1630–1699), pastor of a large Nonconformist congregation at Stepney.

Silenced by the Act of Uniformity in 1662 yet continuing to preach.

Author of The Almost Christian Discovered, from Agrippa’s words in Act 26:28.

He anatomized the self-deceived professor who has form without saving grace.

His doctrine rested on regeneration as the sovereign work of the Spirit (Joh 3:3).

📖 Key Scripture

Act 26:28 — "Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian."

Joh 3:3 — "Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."

2Co 13:5 — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?"

Mat 7:21 — "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Mead’s warning against the “almost Christian” is recovered against an age that calls every professor saved and never tests the heart.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet Mead’s subject cuts directly against the modern aversion to self-examination, which treats any call to prove one’s faith as harsh or judgmental. Mead, following Paul’s charge to examine ourselves, showed how far a man may go in religion—in knowledge, profession, even reformation—and yet remain unconverted. To flatter the almost Christian into false peace is the cruelest kindness; to discover him is mercy.

The lesson to recover is the necessity of the new birth and the duty of honest self-examination. Mead teaches that the gate to false hope is wide, and that many who say “Lord, Lord” have never been made new by the Spirit. The remedy is not to multiply outward religion but to be born again, and to prove, by Scripture and conscience, whether Christ be truly formed within.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Matthew means “gift of the LORD”; Mead denotes a meadow.

expand to see more

Matthew — from Hebrew Mattithyahu, “gift of the LORD.”

Mead, from Old English mæd, “a meadow, a tract of grassland.”

Almost, from all and most, “very nearly,” the perilous nearness of Agrippa (Act 26:28).

Hypocrite, from the Greek hypokritēs, “an actor,” one who plays a part not truly his own.

Regeneration, from the Latin regeneratio, “a being born again” (Joh 3:3).

Usage

"Matthew Mead exposed the man who is almost, but not altogether, a Christian."

"Silenced in 1662, Matthew Mead still gathered a great congregation at Stepney."

"Few books search the conscience like Matthew Mead’s Almost Christian Discovered."
